claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by kinetically controlled stochastic atomic mixing.
Kinetic atomic mixing locks the constituent elements into a homogeneous metastable alloy configuration.
A brief, high-intensity energy input produces rapid atomic mobility and mixing in the precursor state.
Rapid processing freezes a random elemental distribution before thermodynamically driven segregation and phase separation occur.
The precursor is uniformly mixed, with its constituent elements evenly distributed before alloying.
A brief high-energy pulse followed by immediate quenching can freeze the resulting multielement structure.
Diffusion length and the available mixing time mediate whether a homogeneous alloy forms.
A short-time stochastic atomic reorganization homogenizes the alloy before phase separation can dominate.
Within a narrow processing-time window, stochastic atomic motion enables balanced random diffusion of the constituent atoms.
Molecular-dynamics simulation studies reveal the proposed stochastic atomic motions.
Rapid motion followed by quenching prevents equilibrium segregation and phase separation.
Rapid-pulse processing will produce nanoparticles with a more homogeneous elemental distribution than slower, prolonged heating.
Rapid-pulse processing will produce greater exposed surface sites than slower, prolonged heating.
Under the slower-heating baseline, thermodynamically driven diffusion causes phase separation and elemental clustering.
The hypothesis applies primarily to multimetal systems, especially noble-metal systems containing at least five interacting elements, whose diffusion kinetics can be modulated by rapid processing.
The hypothesis may not apply when substrate interactions, extreme differences in elemental melting points, or competing stabilizing interactions dominate mixing dynamics.
The required pulse intensity and duration and the effects of specific element–element interactions are uncertain.
